Knidos was first founded in the Burgaz district on the Dalacak cape, 1.5 km  northeast of  
today's  center  of  Datça.  Later  it  was  moved  to  the  Tekir  Cape  on  the  western  tip  of  the  
peninsula. Knidos was a city advanced in science, architecture, and arts. Eudoxus, a great  
astronomer and mathematician of history, Euryphon, the famous painter Polygnotos, and  
Sostratos, the architect of the Alexandria Lighthouse, which was one of the seven wonders  
of the world, lived here. Euryphon and his students established the second-largest medical  
school  of  their  time  in  Knidos.  The  sun  clock,  developed  by  Eudoxus  and  a  significant  
invention of its era, can still be seen at the archaeological site.
Historian Strabo compares the city to a theatre rising from the coast towards the Acropolis.  
The peninsula, which divides the inner and outer ports, has special buildings, and the slopes  
rising from the inner harbor to the Acropolis have buildings serving the community. Four main  
streets,  10  meters  wide,  run  east-west  and  are  placed  flat  on  the  terraces.  Connections  
between streets are provided by stairs and inclined streets. The city is surrounded by walls  
that extend up to 4 km. It covers a vast area between the military port and the Acropolis, as  
well as the commercial port to the south. The peninsula, known as Deveboynu, used to be  
an island. Its head was connected to the mainland, and artificial ports were formed on both  
sides. A canal was opened for passage on the fill area. The northern port was used for military  
purposes, and there were round control towers on both sides, and its mouth was closed with  
a chain. The control tower in the south is still standing today. The southern inner harbor was  
larger and served as a port for commercial ships.

## [PDF page 9]
Knidos has two theaters, one with a capacity of 20,000 and the other with a capacity of 5,000.  
The smaller one is located in the south, near the commercial port. The large theater on the  
Acropolis has not survived to this day because its stones and marbles were transported by  
ships in the 19th century. The most beautiful point of the archaeological site is the Aphrodite  
Temple,  which  dominates  both  harbors.  The  temple,  which  was  circular  in  plan,  had  a  
diameter of 17 meters. The Aphrodite statue was in the middle of the temple, and the doors  
opened towards the statue. Today, only the pedestal of the statue can be seen.
One of the interesting points of the archaeological site tour is the sun clock that shows the  
seasons and time. There is an Apollo Temple at the top, and the city rises towards it like a  
theater.  The  Corinth  Temple,  located  just  above  the  theater  below,  was  the  work  of  the  
architect Stratos. In the early Christian period, a church was built on the Doric temple located  
on the terrace in the middle of the road leading to the Apollo Temple. The colorful mosaic-  
covered floors of the churches built in the archaeological site can still be seen today. The  
Stoa, which was built by Sostratos, Knidos's famous architect, in the 3rd century BC, has  
been undergoing rescue excavations since 1996, and two-thirds of it have been completed  
to this day. The 113-meter-long and 16-meter-wide structure had small rooms measuring  
5x3.80 m. All rooms faced south. The artifacts found from the rescue excavations carried out  
in the city are exhibited in the small museum at the archaeological site.
www.lalunasailing.com  info@lalunasailing.com  9

## [PDF page 10]
ÇİFTLİK  
Çiftlik is a popular bay, also known as Gerbekse among locals, and is one of the favorite  
harbors for yachts going on a blue voyage. Located in the Gerbekse Cove, which extends  
like  a  tongue  into  the  sea  and  is  sheltered  from  the  wind,  there  are  several  piers  and  
restaurants on the shore. On top of the hill, there is a castle, ancient ruins, and a church.  
Sometimes, boat captains witness a wedding ceremony for newlywed foreign tourists who  
are impressed by the beauty of the church. As you climb towards the hills, the steep and  
rugged cliffs of Gerbekse Cove, which become even more beautiful among pine and olive  
trees, are currently untouched.
The region's season lasts until November 15th, and it is protected from the prevailing winds.  
The coastline is small and pebbly, with a depth of 5-7 meters for yachts, and has good anchor  
holding  capability.  The  interesting  rock  structure  of  Ince  Ada  (Thin  Island)  also  inspires  
admiration, in addition to the beauty of Gerbekse Cove.
BOZUKKALE  
Bozukkale  is  a  beautiful  cove  located  between  Değirmenburnu  and  Kaleburun  in  the  
Bozburun Peninsula. It is a popular stop for yachts and boats during their blue voyage due  
to its sheltered position against the winds. Bozukkale is also known as "Bozuk Bükü" among  
sailors. The cove is surrounded by olive groves and Mediterranean vegetation, making it a  
hidden paradise.

## [PDF page 10]
Upon entering the cove by boat, visitors can see the defense walls and towers surrounding  
the hills. The ancient fortress of Loryma is located among the ruins in Bozukkale, and some  
historians  suggest  that  it hosted  the  Athenian  navy  in  1412  BC.  The  cove  was  also  an  
important gathering point for ships before the Knidos sea battle in 395 BC.  
There are three restaurants that serve yachts in the clear waters of the cove. Behind the  
restaurants, on the top of the hill to the north of the cove, there is another castle ruin. The  
ancient city of Loryma (Bozukkale) was the center of the Rhodian peraias in the 10th century  
BC, but little information is available about its history. The rectangular fortress with walls and  
towers is still in good condition, with nine towers around it. It is believed that the castle was  
a defense unit against the opposite shore of Rhodes.
Next  to  Bozukkale  are  Korsan  Koyu  and  Serçe  Limanı.  Serçe  Limanı  is  famous  for  a  
shipwreck from the Fatimid dynasty in the 11th century AD that was carrying glass stones to  
be worked in Byzantine workshops. The historical value of this shipwreck, recovered through  
underwater  excavations,  is  on  display  at  the  Bodrum  Museum.  In  the  past,  there  was  a  
shipyard at Oplosika Bükü, the name given to Bozukkale in English nautical charts. Due to  
its geographical location and the narrowness of the harbor entrance, Athens ships also used  
this harbor during the Peloponnesian Wars

## [PDF page 10]
SYMI  
Symi, the most beautiful and well-maintained of the Greek islands, was once the richest of  
12 islands in the 17th century due to its sponge trade and shipyards producing 500 ships  
annually. Now, it relies solely on tourism for its economy. As Halikarnas Fisherman put it,  
"Symi's saddle is similar to Datça's." If you ever find yourself on Symi, or as the Ottomans  
called  it,  Sömbeki,  take  a  look  at  the  saddle  of  the  donkeys  or  mules -  you'll  notice  the

#### 36Old Fortress and New Fortress in Corfu, Greece
Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea and also the name of its largest city. The Old Fortress in the center dates back to the 6th century during the Byzantine Period when this town was called Koryfo (means summit) or Corcyra in Latin. The early fortification was expanded during the 12th century, significantly replaced during the Republic of Venice’s rule from 1386 – 1797 and then extensively modified by the British. The Venetians also constructed the New Fortress on the left during the mid-16th century. Most of what is seen today was constructed while Corfu was a protectorate of the United Kingdom from 1815 until 1864. Both fortifications are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This view from the Bay of Garitsa makes it easy to see why the Greek’s call this Kastropolis or Castle City.
Ikoumenikou Patriarchou Athinagora, Kerkira 491 00, Greece  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 37Close Up of Loggerhead Sea Turtle in Argostoli, Greece
Loggerhead sea turtles regularly breed in the Koutavos Lagoon nature reserve in Argostoli, Greece during the spring and summer months. These magnificent marine creatures typically weigh more than 300 pounds and can live up to 65 years. Their head and shells glow with a rainbow of colors as they swim in the sapphire waters surrounding the Ionian Islands.
Ioannou Metaxa & Kerkiras, Argostoli 281 00, Greece  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 38The Parthenon Temple on the Athenian Acropolis in Athens, Greece
This is the world’s most famous Doric temple. The Parthenon was dedicated to the goddess Athena when it was built on a citadel overlooking Athens, Greece. It is one of several archaeological ruins at the Acropolis of Athens. Others include temples and sanctuaries plus two theaters and remnants of other structures. Most of these buildings were constructed during the 5th century BC.
The Parthenon Temple, Zeus' Triangle, Athina 105 58, Greece  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 39Petros the Pelican in Mykonos, Greece
In 1954, a fisherman found an injured great white pelican and nursed him back to health. For over 30 years, Petros the Pelican was a celebrity and the official mascot of Mykonos Island. After he was killed by a car in 1985, his legacy lived on when three other pelicans became permanent residents. Jackie Kennedy-Onassis donated Irene. Another wounded bird is called Nikola. The Hamburg Zoo gifted this one who carries on the name Petros.
Mykonos Waterfront, Mikonos 846 00, Greece  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 40Library of Celsus Ruins in Ephesus, Turkey
Ephesus was a Greek city of half a million people dating back to 10 BC. This archeological gem is located on Turkey’s western coast. Although only a small portion has been excavated, it is an amazing collection of Greek and Roman ruins. The site includes temples, a theater and a basilica. The most impressive is the two-story, 52 foot façade of the Library of Celsus. It once contained over 12,000 scrolls. This magnificent structure was built as a tomb in 117 A.D.
Celsus Library Acarlar Mahallesi, 35920 Selçuk/İzmir, Turkey  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 41Hagia Sophia at Sunset in Istanbul, Turkey
Two previous churches were built on the site of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, Turkey. They were destroyed in 404 and 532 AD. Construction on the replacement required 10,000 workers and materials from quarries in Turkey, Syria and Egypt. When finished in 537, this was the world’s largest cathedral. The architectural masterpiece has a 185 foot dome. 900 years later, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire conquered Constantinople and converted the Byzantine cathedral into an Islamic mosque. In 1934, Ayasofya became a museum and in 2020 it was restored to being a mosque. Hagia Sophia is an incredible landmark to visit.
Sultan Ahmet Mahallesi, Ayasofya Meydanı, 34122 Fatih/İstanbul, Turkey  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 42Dome of the Rock in Moonlight on Temple Mount in Jerusalem, Israel
The Dome of the Rock in the Old City of Jerusalem, Israel is of historical and religious significance to Muslims, Christians and Jews. Built on the Temple Mount in 691 AD, the dome is covered by an aluminum bronze alloy with gold. The greatest significance is inside. The Foundation Stone (the Rock) represents the spiritual joining of Heaven and Earth. This famous landmark is maintained by the Jordanians.
Dome of the Rock, Old City, Jerusalem  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 43Woman Entering Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Museum in Mumbai, India
Mumbai is wall-to-wall people with a population of about 20 million. The atmosphere is crowded and dizzying. But the world’s seventh largest city can also be elegant and beautiful. This woman is wearing a satin saree or sari, an unstitched cloth draped over the body. She is entering the Dr. Bhau Daji Lad Museum. When the city’s oldest museum opened in 1857, it was the Victoria and Albert Museum. The name honored the then reigning queen of the United Kingdom and her husband.
Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Road, Byculla, Mumbai 400027, India  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 44Close Up of Two Yakshas at Grand Palace in Bangkok, Thailand
Yakshas are spiritual beings from Hindu literature. They live in subterranean earth and are protectors of treasures. Some people in India consider them to be deities. They evolved in Thailand to be guardians of gates, temples and royal belongings. They look fierce like a demon. However, in addition to being good warriors, yakshas are considered to be benevolent. This pair is at the base of a golden chedi at the Grand Palace.
Na Phra Lan Rd, Khet Phra Nakhon, Krung Thep Maha Nakhon 10200, Thailand  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 46Southbank and Yarra River in Melbourne, Australia
Southbank is a small neighborhood across the Yarra River from Melbourne’s Central Business District. Despite its .7 square mile size, this former warehouse and wharf precinct has experienced extraordinary development in the last few decades. The revitalization began in the 1980s with the addition of theaters and performing arts venues known as the Arts Centre Melbourne. In the 1990s, the new Southbank Promenade became the impetus for developing waterfront apartments. At the same time, an enormous convention and exhibition center plus the Crown Entertainment Complex were built. During the first decade of the 21st century, office buildings were added and so was Melbourne’s tallest skyscraper. The residential Eureka Tower defines the skyline at 975 feet with 91 floors.
Princes Bridge, St Kilda Rd, Melbourne VIC, 3004 Australia  
Enlarge/SlideshowSee On MapDirections

#### 47Sydney Opera House in Sydney, Australia
The city’s architectural symbol is the Sydney Opera House located on Bennelong Point and jetting into Sydney Harbour. The unique concert hall features concrete shells. They are covered by over a million tiles with a chevron pattern sitting on top of a platform of pink granite. Jørn Utzon won the coveted Pritzker Architecture Prize for his design. Since the $102 million facility opened in 1973, it has hosted countless plays, ballets and musical performances. This UNESCO World Heritage Site is also home to the Sydney Theatre Company, the Sydney Symphony Orchestra and Opera Australia.
Sydney Opera House, Bennelong Point, Sydney NSW 2000, Australia

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Esther 1:2 · Nehemiah 1:1 · Daniel 8:2 · Ezra 4:9Documented Selçuk, İzmir Province, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Ephesus Ephesus is one of the best-preserved ancient cities anywhere, excavated since the 1860s and still worked by the Austrian Archaeological Institute. Its reconstructed Library of Celsus, its great theater seating roughly 25,000, and the marble streets and terraced houses give a vivid picture of a major Greco-Roman port and provincial capital. Nearby stood the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, of which only fragments and a single reassembled column now remain. The New Testament places the apostle Paul here for about three years, and Acts 19 sets a riot of Artemis silversmiths in this very theater; Ephesus is also the first of the seven churches addressed in Revelation. Archaeology confirms the city, its theater, and the Artemis cult that the biblical account presupposes. Acts 19 · 1 Corinthians 15:32 · Ephesians 1:1 · Revelation 2:1-7Documented İzmir, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Smyrna (Izmir) Smyrna is modern İzmir, a large Turkish city that has been continuously inhabited for millennia — which means the ancient city lies mostly buried beneath a living metropolis rather than exposed like Ephesus. The main excavated remnant is the Roman agora at the foot of Pagos Hill, a marketplace and civic center rebuilt under Marcus Aurelius after a destructive earthquake in 178 AD, with its columned basilica, arches, and vaulted lower level still standing. Inscriptions found there even record cities across the empire sending earthquake relief. In Revelation 2:8-11 Smyrna is the church told to 'be faithful unto death,' and Christian tradition remembers the later martyrdom of its bishop Polycarp. Archaeology confirms that ancient Smyrna was a real, prosperous seaport whose civic core can still be visited.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 2:8-11Documented Bergama, İzmir Province, western Turkey Pergamon (Bergama) Pergamon crowns a steep andesite mesa above the modern town of Bergama, its acropolis terraced up more than 300 meters of hillside. Its most dramatic monument is the theater — one of the steepest in the world, cut into the slope with 78 rows for roughly 10,000 spectators. Here too stood the Great Altar, commonly associated with Zeus and Athena and famous for its Gigantomachy frieze; excavated in the 1880s, it was carried off and reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. The city also held the Asclepieion healing sanctuary, where the physician Galen worked, and was an early center of the Roman imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17 addresses the church at Pergamon as living 'where Satan's throne is' — a phrase interpreters have variously linked to the towering Zeus altar or to the imperial cult. Archaeology richly confirms the altar, the theater, and the imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17Documented Tradition Manisa Province, western Türkiye Thyatira (Akhisar) Thyatira was a Greco-Roman city on the Lydia–Mysia border, now buried beneath the modern town of Akhisar. It was known in antiquity for its trade guilds, especially dyers and a purple-cloth trade — the same craft as Lydia, the God-fearing 'seller of purple' from Thyatira whom Paul met at Philippi in Acts 16. In Revelation it is one of the seven churches addressed by John, receiving both praise and a sharp rebuke. What survives today is modest: a partly excavated archaeological park in the middle of Akhisar with a colonnaded street and a large apsidal building often called a basilica, alongside the town's museum. Excavations began under Turkish archaeologists in the 1960s and resumed in 2011, but only a small fraction of the ancient city is exposed. The site is genuine, but visitors should keep expectations modest — the ruins are sparse and hemmed in by the modern town.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 2:18-29 · Acts 16:14Documented Manisa Province, western Türkiye Sardis (Sart) Sardis was the capital of ancient Lydia and the city of King Croesus, legendary for its wealth and among the first places to mint coined money. It is one of the most richly excavated sites of Asia Minor: the enormous, unfinished Temple of Artemis still stands with towering columns, and a Roman bath-gymnasium complex has been substantially reconstructed. Its most celebrated find is the synagogue — discovered by chance in 1962 during Harvard-Cornell excavations — one of the largest and best-preserved ancient synagogues ever found, over 90 meters long with mosaic floors and dozens of Greek inscriptions. In Revelation, Sardis is the church warned that it has 'a name that it is alive, but it is dead.' The archaeology here is genuinely magnificent and abundant. But the standing monuments are civic and religious buildings of the pagan and Jewish city; the Revelation letter itself speaks to a Christian congregation, not to any building that has been dug up. Revelation 3:1-6Documented Tradition Manisa Province, western Türkiye Philadelphia (Alaşehir) Philadelphia was a Hellenistic-founded city on a major road through Lydia, an earthquake-prone region whose people repeatedly rebuilt after the ground shook. It survives today as the modern town of Alaşehir, and little of the ancient city is visible. In Revelation it is one of only two of the seven churches to receive praise and no rebuke, promised an 'open door' and told that the faithful will be made 'a pillar in the temple of my God.' Fittingly, the most conspicuous ruin is a set of massive brick-and-stone pillars — three surviving supports of a Byzantine basilica traditionally called the Church of St. John, built centuries after the New Testament in the late 6th or early 7th century. The ancient city is well attested in history, but on the ground it is sparsely visible: mostly these towering pillars rather than an extensive excavated cityscape.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 3:7-13Documented Lycus Valley, near Denizli, Turkey Laodicea on the Lycus Laodicea was a wealthy Roman city in the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, and it is the last of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, famously rebuked as 'lukewarm... neither hot nor cold.' Decades of excavation, led in recent years by Celal Şimşek, have uncovered a remarkably complete city: two theaters, a large stadium, monumental colonnaded avenues, agoras, bath complexes, temples, and several early churches. Archaeologists have also traced its water infrastructure, including an aqueduct and a pressurized siphon system that piped water into the city. A common devotional reading ties the 'lukewarm' image to tepid piped water, imagined as arriving between the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis and colder sources elsewhere. The ruins and the water system are unmistakably real and well documented. The specific hot-cold-lukewarm water explanation, however, is an interpretation rather than an established fact. Revelation 3:14-22 · Colossians 4:16Tradition Dodecanese, Aegean Sea, Greece Patmos and the Cave of the Apocalypse Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean where, according to Revelation 1:9, John was 'on the island called Patmos because of the word of God' and received the visions recorded in the book. The island itself is real, and Roman-era relegation (exile) to Aegean islands is a documented historical practice, making a first-century exile there entirely plausible. On the slope between the harbor and the hilltop town of Chora, the 'Cave of the Apocalypse' is venerated as the very spot where John received his vision. Crowning the island is the fortress-like Monastery of Saint John the Theologian, founded in 1088, whose library preserves manuscripts going back centuries. Together the cave, monastery, and historic town form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The island and the possibility of exile are historically credible; the identification of one specific cave rests on later Byzantine and medieval tradition rather than physical evidence.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 1:9Documented Athens, Attica, Greece The Areopagus in Athens Athens is where Acts 17 places Paul's address to the philosophers, prompted by an altar he saw inscribed 'to an unknown god.' The city of that era is superbly documented: the Acropolis with the Parthenon, the sprawling Agora where Paul is said to have debated daily, and the Areopagus, a bare rock outcrop just below the Acropolis. The name Areopagus ('Hill of Ares,' rendered 'Mars Hill' in older translations) belonged both to the rock and to the venerable Athenian council that met in connection with it. Ancient Athens was indeed saturated with shrines, statues, and altars to many gods, and altars to unnamed or 'unknown' deities are attested in Greek religious practice. The city, its dense religious landscape, and the Areopagus are all genuine and well attested. Paul's speech itself is Acts' narrative, set convincingly against that real backdrop. Acts 17:16-34Documented Debated Peloponnese, Greece Ancient Corinth Corinth was a wealthy Roman colonial city on the isthmus linking mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, and Acts 18 says Paul stayed here about eighteen months, working as a tentmaker and founding the church he later wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians to. The site has been excavated since 1896 (chiefly by the American School), exposing the sixth-century-BC Temple of Apollo with its surviving Doric columns, the sprawling forum, and the bema, a raised public platform later marked as a church of the Apostle Paul. Two inscriptions give Corinth unusual evidential weight. The Gallio Inscription from Delphi names Lucius Junius Gallio as proconsul of Achaia and, by tying his term to Emperor Claudius's reign, fixes it to roughly AD 51-52, which anchors Paul's trial before Gallio (Acts 18:12) and with it much of Pauline chronology. A separate Latin paving inscription found near the theater names an Erastus who funded work in return for his aedileship, which some connect to Erastus the city treasurer in Romans 16:23.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Acts 18:1-18 · 1 Corinthians 1:1-2 · Romans 16:23Documented Tradition Eastern Macedonia, Greece Philippi Philippi was a Roman colony astride the Via Egnatia in eastern Macedonia, and Acts 16 records it as the setting of Paul's first recorded preaching in Europe, including the conversion of Lydia the cloth-dealer and the jailer, and it is the community Paul addresses in his letter to the Philippians. Excavations by the French School (from 1914) and later Greek archaeologists have uncovered the terraced Roman forum built between the reigns of Claudius and Antoninus Pius, an enlarged theater, and several grand early-Christian basilicas, one of whose mosaic floors names Paul. The archaeological site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016 for its Roman architecture and early-Christian importance. Visitors are also shown a crypt venerated as the place of Paul's imprisonment and a riverside spot commemorated as where Lydia was baptized. The Roman colony and its public buildings are solidly attested by excavation; the specific devotional sites rest on later tradition rather than proof. Acts 16:11-40 · Philippians 1:1Documented Central Macedonia, Greece Thessalonica Thessalonica, the modern city of Thessaloniki, was a major Roman port on the Via Egnatia and the capital of the province of Macedonia, and Acts 17 describes Paul preaching in its synagogue before a riot forced him out; it received two of his letters, 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Because a large living city has grown continuously on the ancient site, the classical remains are only partly exposed, but the Roman-era forum (ancient agora), the fourth-century Rotunda built under Galerius, and the nearby Arch of Galerius still survive above ground. A notable accuracy point concerns terminology: Acts 17:6 calls the city's magistrates 'politarchs,' a title once thought unattested and even doubted by some critics. Inscriptions from Thessalonica and Macedonia, however, have since documented that 'politarch' was a genuine local civic title, matching Luke's usage precisely. The ancient city is unquestionably real; much of it simply lies beneath the modern one.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Acts 17:1-9 · 1 Thessalonians 1:1 · 2 Thessalonians 1:1Documented Tradition Central Macedonia, Greece Berea (Veria) Berea is modern Veria, a living city in northern Greece continuously inhabited since antiquity. In Acts 17 Paul, Silas and Timothy came here by night after leaving Thessalonica, and Luke praises the Bereans as 'noble' or fair-minded because they 'examined the Scriptures daily' to test what Paul taught. The city is genuinely ancient — settlement traces reach back roughly three thousand years — but because the modern town sits directly on top of it, very little of the classical and Roman town has been excavated or exposed. In the city today there is a commemorative monument known as the Bema of the Apostle Paul, decorated with mosaics and marking where tradition says he preached. It is worth being plain: that monument is a modern devotional shrine built by the Greek Orthodox Church, not an excavated first-century site, and the exact location of the synagogue Paul visited is not archaeologically known. What is well founded is simply that Berea was a real Macedonian city and a documented stop on Paul's journey. Acts 17:10-12 · Acts 20:4Documented Tradition Italy Rome Rome was the capital of the empire and the destination of Paul's final recorded journey: Acts 28 describes him arriving as a prisoner and spending two years under guard, preaching freely in his own rented lodging. Christian tradition holds that both Paul and Peter were martyred in Rome, and the city preserves an extraordinary wealth of documented first-century remains — the Forum, the streets and monuments Paul would have known, and later the catacombs used by the early Christian community. Two sites carry strong tradition but weaker proof. The Mamertine Prison is venerated as the place Peter and Paul were held, though there is no evidence either apostle was actually imprisoned there. Beneath St. Peter's Basilica, the 1940s Vatican excavations uncovered a genuine Roman necropolis and a small second-century shrine with graffiti, which the Church has identified as the tomb of Peter. That Rome had a real, early Christian presence is richly attested; the specific identification of Peter's bones and the Mamertine imprisonment remain traditions supported by early testimony rather than settled fact.

Historian Strabo compares the city to a theatre rising from the coast towards the Acropolis.  
The peninsula, which divides the inner and outer ports, has special buildings, and the slopes  
rising from the inner harbor to the Acropolis have buildings serving the community. Four main  
streets,  10  meters  wide,  run  east-west  and  are  placed  flat  on  the  terraces.  Connections  
between streets are provided by stairs and inclined streets. The city is surrounded by walls  
that extend up to 4 km. It covers a vast area between the military port and the Acropolis, as  
well as the commercial port to the south. The peninsula, known as Deveboynu, used to be  
an island. Its head was connected to the mainland, and artificial ports were formed on both  
sides. A canal was opened for passage on the fill area. The northern port was used for military  
purposes, and there were round control towers on both sides, and its mouth was closed with  
a chain. The control tower in the south is still standing today. The southern inner harbor was  
larger and served as a port for commercial ships.
texts.10:
## [PDF page 9]
Knidos has two theaters, one with a capacity of 20,000 and the other with a capacity of 5,000.  
The smaller one is located in the south, near the commercial port. The large theater on the  
Acropolis has not survived to this day because its stones and marbles were transported by  
ships in the 19th century. The most beautiful point of the archaeological site is the Aphrodite  
Temple,  which  dominates  both  harbors.  The  temple,  which  was  circular  in  plan,  had  a  
diameter of 17 meters. The Aphrodite statue was in the middle of the temple, and the doors  
opened towards the statue. Today, only the pedestal of the statue can be seen.
One of the interesting points of the archaeological site tour is the sun clock that shows the  
seasons and time. There is an Apollo Temple at the top, and the city rises towards it like a  
theater.  The  Corinth  Temple,  located  just  above  the  theater  below,  was  the  work  of  the  
architect Stratos. In the early Christian period, a church was built on the Doric temple located  
on the terrace in the middle of the road leading to the Apollo Temple. The colorful mosaic-  
covered floors of the churches built in the archaeological site can still be seen today. The  
Stoa, which was built by Sostratos, Knidos's famous architect, in the 3rd century BC, has  
been undergoing rescue excavations since 1996, and two-thirds of it have been completed  
to this day. The 113-meter-long and 16-meter-wide structure had small rooms measuring  
5x3.80 m. All rooms faced south. The artifacts found from the rescue excavations carried out  
in the city are exhibited in the small museum at the archaeological site.

## [PDF page 10]
ÇİFTLİK  
Çiftlik is a popular bay, also known as Gerbekse among locals, and is one of the favorite  
harbors for yachts going on a blue voyage. Located in the Gerbekse Cove, which extends  
like  a  tongue  into  the  sea  and  is  sheltered  from  the  wind,  there  are  several  piers  and  
restaurants on the shore. On top of the hill, there is a castle, ancient ruins, and a church.  
Sometimes, boat captains witness a wedding ceremony for newlywed foreign tourists who  
are impressed by the beauty of the church. As you climb towards the hills, the steep and  
rugged cliffs of Gerbekse Cove, which become even more beautiful among pine and olive  
trees, are currently untouched.
The region's season lasts until November 15th, and it is protected from the prevailing winds.  
The coastline is small and pebbly, with a depth of 5-7 meters for yachts, and has good anchor  
holding  capability.  The  interesting  rock  structure  of  Ince  Ada  (Thin  Island)  also  inspires  
admiration, in addition to the beauty of Gerbekse Cove.
BOZUKKALE  
Bozukkale  is  a  beautiful  cove  located  between  Değirmenburnu  and  Kaleburun  in  the  
Bozburun Peninsula. It is a popular stop for yachts and boats during their blue voyage due  
to its sheltered position against the winds. Bozukkale is also known as "Bozuk Bükü" among  
sailors. The cove is surrounded by olive groves and Mediterranean vegetation, making it a  
hidden paradise.
texts.12:
## [PDF page 10]
Upon entering the cove by boat, visitors can see the defense walls and towers surrounding  
the hills. The ancient fortress of Loryma is located among the ruins in Bozukkale, and some  
historians  suggest  that  it hosted  the  Athenian  navy  in  1412  BC.  The  cove  was  also  an  
important gathering point for ships before the Knidos sea battle in 395 BC.  
There are three restaurants that serve yachts in the clear waters of the cove. Behind the  
restaurants, on the top of the hill to the north of the cove, there is another castle ruin. The  
ancient city of Loryma (Bozukkale) was the center of the Rhodian peraias in the 10th century  
BC, but little information is available about its history. The rectangular fortress with walls and  
towers is still in good condition, with nine towers around it. It is believed that the castle was  
a defense unit against the opposite shore of Rhodes.
Next  to  Bozukkale  are  Korsan  Koyu  and  Serçe  Limanı.  Serçe  Limanı  is  famous  for  a  
shipwreck from the Fatimid dynasty in the 11th century AD that was carrying glass stones to  
be worked in Byzantine workshops. The historical value of this shipwreck, recovered through  
underwater  excavations,  is  on  display  at  the  Bodrum  Museum.  In  the  past,  there  was  a  
shipyard at Oplosika Bükü, the name given to Bozukkale in English nautical charts. Due to  
its geographical location and the narrowness of the harbor entrance, Athens ships also used  
this harbor during the Peloponnesian Wars

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Esther 1:2 · Nehemiah 1:1 · Daniel 8:2 · Ezra 4:9Documented Selçuk, İzmir Province, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Ephesus Ephesus is one of the best-preserved ancient cities anywhere, excavated since the 1860s and still worked by the Austrian Archaeological Institute. Its reconstructed Library of Celsus, its great theater seating roughly 25,000, and the marble streets and terraced houses give a vivid picture of a major Greco-Roman port and provincial capital. Nearby stood the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, of which only fragments and a single reassembled column now remain. The New Testament places the apostle Paul here for about three years, and Acts 19 sets a riot of Artemis silversmiths in this very theater; Ephesus is also the first of the seven churches addressed in Revelation. Archaeology confirms the city, its theater, and the Artemis cult that the biblical account presupposes. Acts 19 · 1 Corinthians 15:32 · Ephesians 1:1 · Revelation 2:1-7Documented İzmir, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Smyrna (Izmir) Smyrna is modern İzmir, a large Turkish city that has been continuously inhabited for millennia — which means the ancient city lies mostly buried beneath a living metropolis rather than exposed like Ephesus. The main excavated remnant is the Roman agora at the foot of Pagos Hill, a marketplace and civic center rebuilt under Marcus Aurelius after a destructive earthquake in 178 AD, with its columned basilica, arches, and vaulted lower level still standing. Inscriptions found there even record cities across the empire sending earthquake relief. In Revelation 2:8-11 Smyrna is the church told to 'be faithful unto death,' and Christian tradition remembers the later martyrdom of its bishop Polycarp. Archaeology confirms that ancient Smyrna was a real, prosperous seaport whose civic core can still be visited.
texts.26:
# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 2:8-11Documented Bergama, İzmir Province, western Turkey Pergamon (Bergama) Pergamon crowns a steep andesite mesa above the modern town of Bergama, its acropolis terraced up more than 300 meters of hillside. Its most dramatic monument is the theater — one of the steepest in the world, cut into the slope with 78 rows for roughly 10,000 spectators. Here too stood the Great Altar, commonly associated with Zeus and Athena and famous for its Gigantomachy frieze; excavated in the 1880s, it was carried off and reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. The city also held the Asclepieion healing sanctuary, where the physician Galen worked, and was an early center of the Roman imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17 addresses the church at Pergamon as living 'where Satan's throne is' — a phrase interpreters have variously linked to the towering Zeus altar or to the imperial cult. Archaeology richly confirms the altar, the theater, and the imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17Documented Tradition Manisa Province, western Türkiye Thyatira (Akhisar) Thyatira was a Greco-Roman city on the Lydia–Mysia border, now buried beneath the modern town of Akhisar. It was known in antiquity for its trade guilds, especially dyers and a purple-cloth trade — the same craft as Lydia, the God-fearing 'seller of purple' from Thyatira whom Paul met at Philippi in Acts 16. In Revelation it is one of the seven churches addressed by John, receiving both praise and a sharp rebuke. What survives today is modest: a partly excavated archaeological park in the middle of Akhisar with a colonnaded street and a large apsidal building often called a basilica, alongside the town's museum. Excavations began under Turkish archaeologists in the 1960s and resumed in 2011, but only a small fraction of the ancient city is exposed. The site is genuine, but visitors should keep expectations modest — the ruins are sparse and hemmed in by the modern town.
texts.27:
# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 2:18-29 · Acts 16:14Documented Manisa Province, western Türkiye Sardis (Sart) Sardis was the capital of ancient Lydia and the city of King Croesus, legendary for its wealth and among the first places to mint coined money. It is one of the most richly excavated sites of Asia Minor: the enormous, unfinished Temple of Artemis still stands with towering columns, and a Roman bath-gymnasium complex has been substantially reconstructed. Its most celebrated find is the synagogue — discovered by chance in 1962 during Harvard-Cornell excavations — one of the largest and best-preserved ancient synagogues ever found, over 90 meters long with mosaic floors and dozens of Greek inscriptions. In Revelation, Sardis is the church warned that it has 'a name that it is alive, but it is dead.' The archaeology here is genuinely magnificent and abundant. But the standing monuments are civic and religious buildings of the pagan and Jewish city; the Revelation letter itself speaks to a Christian congregation, not to any building that has been dug up. Revelation 3:1-6Documented Tradition Manisa Province, western Türkiye Philadelphia (Alaşehir) Philadelphia was a Hellenistic-founded city on a major road through Lydia, an earthquake-prone region whose people repeatedly rebuilt after the ground shook. It survives today as the modern town of Alaşehir, and little of the ancient city is visible. In Revelation it is one of only two of the seven churches to receive praise and no rebuke, promised an 'open door' and told that the faithful will be made 'a pillar in the temple of my God.' Fittingly, the most conspicuous ruin is a set of massive brick-and-stone pillars — three surviving supports of a Byzantine basilica traditionally called the Church of St. John, built centuries after the New Testament in the late 6th or early 7th century. The ancient city is well attested in history, but on the ground it is sparsely visible: mostly these towering pillars rather than an extensive excavated cityscape.
texts.28:
# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 3:7-13Documented Lycus Valley, near Denizli, Turkey Laodicea on the Lycus Laodicea was a wealthy Roman city in the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, and it is the last of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, famously rebuked as 'lukewarm... neither hot nor cold.' Decades of excavation, led in recent years by Celal Şimşek, have uncovered a remarkably complete city: two theaters, a large stadium, monumental colonnaded avenues, agoras, bath complexes, temples, and several early churches. Archaeologists have also traced its water infrastructure, including an aqueduct and a pressurized siphon system that piped water into the city. A common devotional reading ties the 'lukewarm' image to tepid piped water, imagined as arriving between the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis and colder sources elsewhere. The ruins and the water system are unmistakably real and well documented. The specific hot-cold-lukewarm water explanation, however, is an interpretation rather than an established fact. Revelation 3:14-22 · Colossians 4:16Tradition Dodecanese, Aegean Sea, Greece Patmos and the Cave of the Apocalypse Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean where, according to Revelation 1:9, John was 'on the island called Patmos because of the word of God' and received the visions recorded in the book. The island itself is real, and Roman-era relegation (exile) to Aegean islands is a documented historical practice, making a first-century exile there entirely plausible. On the slope between the harbor and the hilltop town of Chora, the 'Cave of the Apocalypse' is venerated as the very spot where John received his vision. Crowning the island is the fortress-like Monastery of Saint John the Theologian, founded in 1088, whose library preserves manuscripts going back centuries. Together the cave, monastery, and historic town form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The island and the possibility of exile are historically credible; the identification of one specific cave rests on later Byzantine and medieval tradition rather than physical evidence.
texts.29:
# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Revelation 1:9Documented Athens, Attica, Greece The Areopagus in Athens Athens is where Acts 17 places Paul's address to the philosophers, prompted by an altar he saw inscribed 'to an unknown god.' The city of that era is superbly documented: the Acropolis with the Parthenon, the sprawling Agora where Paul is said to have debated daily, and the Areopagus, a bare rock outcrop just below the Acropolis. The name Areopagus ('Hill of Ares,' rendered 'Mars Hill' in older translations) belonged both to the rock and to the venerable Athenian council that met in connection with it. Ancient Athens was indeed saturated with shrines, statues, and altars to many gods, and altars to unnamed or 'unknown' deities are attested in Greek religious practice. The city, its dense religious landscape, and the Areopagus are all genuine and well attested. Paul's speech itself is Acts' narrative, set convincingly against that real backdrop. Acts 17:16-34Documented Debated Peloponnese, Greece Ancient Corinth Corinth was a wealthy Roman colonial city on the isthmus linking mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, and Acts 18 says Paul stayed here about eighteen months, working as a tentmaker and founding the church he later wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians to. The site has been excavated since 1896 (chiefly by the American School), exposing the sixth-century-BC Temple of Apollo with its surviving Doric columns, the sprawling forum, and the bema, a raised public platform later marked as a church of the Apostle Paul. Two inscriptions give Corinth unusual evidential weight. The Gallio Inscription from Delphi names Lucius Junius Gallio as proconsul of Achaia and, by tying his term to Emperor Claudius's reign, fixes it to roughly AD 51-52, which anchors Paul's trial before Gallio (Acts 18:12) and with it much of Pauline chronology. A separate Latin paving inscription found near the theater names an Erastus who funded work in return for his aedileship, which some connect to Erastus the city treasurer in Romans 16:23.

# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Acts 18:1-18 · 1 Corinthians 1:1-2 · Romans 16:23Documented Tradition Eastern Macedonia, Greece Philippi Philippi was a Roman colony astride the Via Egnatia in eastern Macedonia, and Acts 16 records it as the setting of Paul's first recorded preaching in Europe, including the conversion of Lydia the cloth-dealer and the jailer, and it is the community Paul addresses in his letter to the Philippians. Excavations by the French School (from 1914) and later Greek archaeologists have uncovered the terraced Roman forum built between the reigns of Claudius and Antoninus Pius, an enlarged theater, and several grand early-Christian basilicas, one of whose mosaic floors names Paul. The archaeological site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016 for its Roman architecture and early-Christian importance. Visitors are also shown a crypt venerated as the place of Paul's imprisonment and a riverside spot commemorated as where Lydia was baptized. The Roman colony and its public buildings are solidly attested by excavation; the specific devotional sites rest on later tradition rather than proof. Acts 16:11-40 · Philippians 1:1Documented Central Macedonia, Greece Thessalonica Thessalonica, the modern city of Thessaloniki, was a major Roman port on the Via Egnatia and the capital of the province of Macedonia, and Acts 17 describes Paul preaching in its synagogue before a riot forced him out; it received two of his letters, 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Because a large living city has grown continuously on the ancient site, the classical remains are only partly exposed, but the Roman-era forum (ancient agora), the fourth-century Rotunda built under Galerius, and the nearby Arch of Galerius still survive above ground. A notable accuracy point concerns terminology: Acts 17:6 calls the city's magistrates 'politarchs,' a title once thought unattested and even doubted by some critics. Inscriptions from Thessalonica and Macedonia, however, have since documented that 'politarch' was a genuine local civic title, matching Luke's usage precisely. The ancient city is unquestionably real; much of it simply lies beneath the modern one.
texts.31:
# What the Ground Remembers
## Places you can stand today
Acts 17:1-9 · 1 Thessalonians 1:1 · 2 Thessalonians 1:1Documented Tradition Central Macedonia, Greece Berea (Veria) Berea is modern Veria, a living city in northern Greece continuously inhabited since antiquity. In Acts 17 Paul, Silas and Timothy came here by night after leaving Thessalonica, and Luke praises the Bereans as 'noble' or fair-minded because they 'examined the Scriptures daily' to test what Paul taught. The city is genuinely ancient — settlement traces reach back roughly three thousand years — but because the modern town sits directly on top of it, very little of the classical and Roman town has been excavated or exposed. In the city today there is a commemorative monument known as the Bema of the Apostle Paul, decorated with mosaics and marking where tradition says he preached. It is worth being plain: that monument is a modern devotional shrine built by the Greek Orthodox Church, not an excavated first-century site, and the exact location of the synagogue Paul visited is not archaeologically known. What is well founded is simply that Berea was a real Macedonian city and a documented stop on Paul's journey. Acts 17:10-12 · Acts 20:4Documented Tradition Italy Rome Rome was the capital of the empire and the destination of Paul's final recorded journey: Acts 28 describes him arriving as a prisoner and spending two years under guard, preaching freely in his own rented lodging. Christian tradition holds that both Paul and Peter were martyred in Rome, and the city preserves an extraordinary wealth of documented first-century remains — the Forum, the streets and monuments Paul would have known, and later the catacombs used by the early Christian community. Two sites carry strong tradition but weaker proof. The Mamertine Prison is venerated as the place Peter and Paul were held, though there is no evidence either apostle was actually imprisoned there. Beneath St. Peter's Basilica, the 1940s Vatican excavations uncovered a genuine Roman necropolis and a small second-century shrine with graffiti, which the Church has identified as the tomb of Peter. That Rome had a real, early Christian presence is richly attested; the specific identification of Peter's bones and the Mamertine imprisonment remain traditions supported by early testimony rather than settled fact.

#### 36Old Fortress and New Fortress in Corfu, Greece
Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea and also the name of its largest city. The Old Fortress in the center dates back to the 6th century during the Byzantine Period when this town was called Koryfo (means summit) or Corcyra in Latin. The early fortification was expanded during the 12th century, significantly replaced during the Republic of Venice’s rule from 1386 – 1797 and then extensively modified by the British. The Venetians also constructed the New Fortress on the left during the mid-16th century. Most of what is seen today was constructed while Corfu was a protectorate of the United Kingdom from 1815 until 1864. Both fortifications are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This view from the Bay of Garitsa makes it easy to see why the Greek’s call this Kastropolis or Castle City.

It is one of several archaeological ruins at the Acropolis of Athens. Others include temples and sanctuaries plus two theaters and remnants of other structures. Most of these buildings were constructed during the 5th century BC.

In 1954, a fisherman found an injured great white pelican and nursed him back to health. For over 30 years, Petros the Pelican was a celebrity and the official mascot of Mykonos Island. After he was killed by a car in 1985, his legacy lived on when three other pelicans became permanent residents. Jackie Kennedy-Onassis donated Irene. Another wounded bird is called Nikola. #### 40Library of Celsus Ruins in Ephesus, Turkey
Ephesus was a Greek city of half a million people dating back to 10 BC. This archeological gem is located on Turkey’s western coast. Although only a small portion has been excavated, it is an amazing collection of Greek and Roman ruins. The site includes temples, a theater and a basilica. The most impressive is the two-story, 52 foot façade of the Library of Celsus. It once contained over 12,000 scrolls. This magnificent structure was built as a tomb in 117 A.D.

#### 41Hagia Sophia at Sunset in Istanbul, Turkey
Two previous churches were built on the site of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, Turkey. They were destroyed in 404 and 532 AD. Construction on the replacement required 10,000 workers and materials from quarries in Turkey, Syria and Egypt. When finished in 537, this was the world’s largest cathedral. The architectural masterpiece has a 185 foot dome. 900 years later, the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire conquered Constantinople and converted the Byzantine cathedral into an Islamic mosque. In 1934, Ayasofya became a museum and in 2020 it was restored to being a mosque. Hagia Sophia is an incredible landmark to visit.

The Dome of the Rock in the Old City of Jerusalem, Israel is of historical and religious significance to Muslims, Christians and Jews. Built on the Temple Mount in 691 AD, the dome is covered by an aluminum bronze alloy with gold. The greatest significance is inside. The Foundation Stone (the Rock) represents the spiritual joining of Heaven and Earth. This famous landmark is maintained by the Jordanians.

Mumbai is wall-to-wall people with a population of about 20 million. The atmosphere is crowded and dizzying. But the world’s seventh largest city can also be elegant and beautiful. #### 44Close Up of Two Yakshas at Grand Palace in Bangkok, Thailand
Yakshas are spiritual beings from Hindu literature. They live in subterranean earth and are protectors of treasures. Some people in India consider them to be deities. They evolved in Thailand to be guardians of gates, temples and royal belongings. They look fierce like a demon. However, in addition to being good warriors, yakshas are considered to be benevolent. #### 46Southbank and Yarra River in Melbourne, Australia
Southbank is a small neighborhood across the Yarra River from Melbourne’s Central Business District. Despite its .7 square mile size, this former warehouse and wharf precinct has experienced extraordinary development in the last few decades. The revitalization began in the 1980s with the addition of theaters and performing arts venues known as the Arts Centre Melbourne. In the 1990s, the new Southbank Promenade became the impetus for developing waterfront apartments. At the same time, an enormous convention and exhibition center plus the Crown Entertainment Complex were built. During the first decade of the 21st century, office buildings were added and so was Melbourne’s tallest skyscraper. The residential Eureka Tower defines the skyline at 975 feet with 91 floors.

#### 47Sydney Opera House in Sydney, Australia
The city’s architectural symbol is the Sydney Opera House located on Bennelong Point and jetting into Sydney Harbour. The unique concert hall features concrete shells. They are covered by over a million tiles with a chevron pattern sitting on top of a platform of pink granite. Jørn Utzon won the coveted Pritzker Architecture Prize for his design. Since the $102 million facility opened in 1973, it has hosted countless plays, ballets and musical performances. This UNESCO World Heritage Site is also home to the Sydney Theatre Company, the Sydney Symphony Orchestra and Opera Australia.

## [PDF page 9]
Knidos
Knidos was first founded in the Burgaz district on the Dalacak cape, 1.5 km  northeast of  
today's  center  of  Datça.  Later  it  was  moved  to  the  Tekir  Cape  on  the  western  tip  of  the  
peninsula. Knidos was a city advanced in science, architecture, and arts. Eudoxus, a great  
astronomer and mathematician of history, Euryphon, the famous painter Polygnotos, and  
Sostratos, the architect of the Alexandria Lighthouse, which was one of the seven wonders  
of the world, lived here. Euryphon and his students established the second-largest medical  
school  of  their  time  in  Knidos.  The  sun  clock,  developed  by  Eudoxus  and  a  significant  
invention of its era, can still be seen at the archaeological site.
Historian Strabo compares the city to a theatre rising from the coast towards the Acropolis.  
The peninsula, which divides the inner and outer ports, has special buildings, and the slopes  
rising from the inner harbor to the Acropolis have buildings serving the community. Four main  
streets,  10  meters  wide,  run  east-west  and  are  placed  flat  on  the  terraces.  Connections  
between streets are provided by stairs and inclined streets. The city is surrounded by walls  
that extend up to 4 km. It covers a vast area between the military port and the Acropolis, as  
well as the commercial port to the south. The peninsula, known as Deveboynu, used to be  
an island. Its head was connected to the mainland, and artificial ports were formed on both  
sides. A canal was opened for passage on the fill area. The northern port was used for military  
purposes, and there were round control towers on both sides, and its mouth was closed with  
a chain. The control tower in the south is still standing today. The southern inner harbor was  
larger and served as a port for commercial ships.

## [PDF page 9]
Knidos has two theaters, one with a capacity of 20,000 and the other with a capacity of 5,000.  
The smaller one is located in the south, near the commercial port. The large theater on the  
Acropolis has not survived to this day because its stones and marbles were transported by  
ships in the 19th century. The most beautiful point of the archaeological site is the Aphrodite  
Temple,  which  dominates  both  harbors.  The  temple,  which  was  circular  in  plan,  had  a  
diameter of 17 meters. The Aphrodite statue was in the middle of the temple, and the doors  
opened towards the statue. Today, only the pedestal of the statue can be seen.
One of the interesting points of the archaeological site tour is the sun clock that shows the  
seasons and time. There is an Apollo Temple at the top, and the city rises towards it like a  
theater.  The  Corinth  Temple,  located  just  above  the  theater  below,  was  the  work  of  the  
architect Stratos. In the early Christian period, a church was built on the Doric temple located  
on the terrace in the middle of the road leading to the Apollo Temple. The colorful mosaic-  
covered floors of the churches built in the archaeological site can still be seen today. The  
Stoa, which was built by Sostratos, Knidos's famous architect, in the 3rd century BC, has  
been undergoing rescue excavations since 1996, and two-thirds of it have been completed  
to this day. The 113-meter-long and 16-meter-wide structure had small rooms measuring  
5x3.80 m. All rooms faced south. The artifacts found from the rescue excavations carried out  
in the city are exhibited in the small museum at the archaeological site.

rugged cliffs of Gerbekse Cove, which become even more beautiful among pine and olive

Esther 1:2 · Nehemiah 1:1 · Daniel 8:2 · Ezra 4:9Documented Selçuk, İzmir Province, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Ephesus Ephesus is one of the best-preserved ancient cities anywhere, excavated since the 1860s and still worked by the Austrian Archaeological Institute. Its reconstructed Library of Celsus, its great theater seating roughly 25,000, and the marble streets and terraced houses give a vivid picture of a major Greco-Roman port and provincial capital. Nearby stood the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, of which only fragments and a single reassembled column now remain. The New Testament places the apostle Paul here for about three years, and Acts 19 sets a riot of Artemis silversmiths in this very theater; Ephesus is also the first of the seven churches addressed in Revelation. Archaeology confirms the city, its theater, and the Artemis cult that the biblical account presupposes. Acts 19 · 1 Corinthians 15:32 · Ephesians 1:1 · Revelation 2:1-7Documented İzmir, western Turkey (Aegean coast) Smyrna (Izmir) Smyrna is modern İzmir, a large Turkish city that has been continuously inhabited for millennia — which means the ancient city lies mostly buried beneath a living metropolis rather than exposed like Ephesus. The main excavated remnant is the Roman agora at the foot of Pagos Hill, a marketplace and civic center rebuilt under Marcus Aurelius after a destructive earthquake in 178 AD, with its columned basilica, arches, and vaulted lower level still standing. Inscriptions found there even record cities across the empire sending earthquake relief. In Revelation 2:8-11 Smyrna is the church told to 'be faithful unto death,' and Christian tradition remembers the later martyrdom of its bishop Polycarp. Archaeology confirms that ancient Smyrna was a real, prosperous seaport whose civic core can still be visited.

## Places you can stand today
Revelation 2:8-11Documented Bergama, İzmir Province, western Turkey Pergamon (Bergama) Pergamon crowns a steep andesite mesa above the modern town of Bergama, its acropolis terraced up more than 300 meters of hillside. Its most dramatic monument is the theater — one of the steepest in the world, cut into the slope with 78 rows for roughly 10,000 spectators. Here too stood the Great Altar, commonly associated with Zeus and Athena and famous for its Gigantomachy frieze; excavated in the 1880s, it was carried off and reconstructed in Berlin's Pergamon Museum. The city also held the Asclepieion healing sanctuary, where the physician Galen worked, and was an early center of the Roman imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17 addresses the church at Pergamon as living 'where Satan's throne is' — a phrase interpreters have variously linked to the towering Zeus altar or to the imperial cult. Archaeology richly confirms the altar, the theater, and the imperial cult. Revelation 2:12-17Documented Tradition Manisa Province, western Türkiye Thyatira (Akhisar) Thyatira was a Greco-Roman city on the Lydia–Mysia border, now buried beneath the modern town of Akhisar. It was known in antiquity for its trade guilds, especially dyers and a purple-cloth trade — the same craft as Lydia, the God-fearing 'seller of purple' from Thyatira whom Paul met at Philippi in Acts 16. In Revelation it is one of the seven churches addressed by John, receiving both praise and a sharp rebuke. What survives today is modest: a partly excavated archaeological park in the middle of Akhisar with a colonnaded street and a large apsidal building often called a basilica, alongside the town's museum. Excavations began under Turkish archaeologists in the 1960s and resumed in 2011, but only a small fraction of the ancient city is exposed. The site is genuine, but visitors should keep expectations modest — the ruins are sparse and hemmed in by the modern town.

Revelation 2:18-29 · Acts 16:14Documented Manisa Province, western Türkiye Sardis (Sart) Sardis was the capital of ancient Lydia and the city of King Croesus, legendary for its wealth and among the first places to mint coined money. It is one of the most richly excavated sites of Asia Minor: the enormous, unfinished Temple of Artemis still stands with towering columns, and a Roman bath-gymnasium complex has been substantially reconstructed. Its most celebrated find is the synagogue — discovered by chance in 1962 during Harvard-Cornell excavations — one of the largest and best-preserved ancient synagogues ever found, over 90 meters long with mosaic floors and dozens of Greek inscriptions. In Revelation, Sardis is the church warned that it has 'a name that it is alive, but it is dead.' The archaeology here is genuinely magnificent and abundant. But the standing monuments are civic and religious buildings of the pagan and Jewish city; the Revelation letter itself speaks to a Christian congregation, not to any building that has been dug up. In Revelation it is one of only two of the seven churches to receive praise and no rebuke, promised an 'open door' and told that the faithful will be made 'a pillar in the temple of my God.' ## Places you can stand today
Revelation 3:7-13Documented Lycus Valley, near Denizli, Turkey Laodicea on the Lycus Laodicea was a wealthy Roman city in the Lycus Valley of Phrygia, and it is the last of the seven churches addressed in Revelation, famously rebuked as 'lukewarm... neither hot nor cold.' Decades of excavation, led in recent years by Celal Şimşek, have uncovered a remarkably complete city: two theaters, a large stadium, monumental colonnaded avenues, agoras, bath complexes, temples, and several early churches. Archaeologists have also traced its water infrastructure, including an aqueduct and a pressurized siphon system that piped water into the city. A common devotional reading ties the 'lukewarm' image to tepid piped water, imagined as arriving between the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis and colder sources elsewhere. The ruins and the water system are unmistakably real and well documented. The specific hot-cold-lukewarm water explanation, however, is an interpretation rather than an established fact. Revelation 3:14-22 · Colossians 4:16Tradition Dodecanese, Aegean Sea, Greece Patmos and the Cave of the Apocalypse Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean where, according to Revelation 1:9, John was 'on the island called Patmos because of the word of God' and received the visions recorded in the book. The island itself is real, and Roman-era relegation (exile) to Aegean islands is a documented historical practice, making a first-century exile there entirely plausible. On the slope between the harbor and the hilltop town of Chora, the 'Cave of the Apocalypse' is venerated as the very spot where John received his vision. Crowning the island is the fortress-like Monastery of Saint John the Theologian, founded in 1088, whose library preserves manuscripts going back centuries. Together the cave, monastery, and historic town form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The island and the possibility of exile are historically credible; the identification of one specific cave rests on later Byzantine and medieval tradition rather than physical evidence.

## Places you can stand today
Revelation 1:9Documented Athens, Attica, Greece The Areopagus in Athens Athens is where Acts 17 places Paul's address to the philosophers, prompted by an altar he saw inscribed 'to an unknown god.' The city of that era is superbly documented: the Acropolis with the Parthenon, the sprawling Agora where Paul is said to have debated daily, and the Areopagus, a bare rock outcrop just below the Acropolis. The name Areopagus ('Hill of Ares,' rendered 'Mars Hill' in older translations) belonged both to the rock and to the venerable Athenian council that met in connection with it. Ancient Athens was indeed saturated with shrines, statues, and altars to many gods, and altars to unnamed or 'unknown' deities are attested in Greek religious practice. The city, its dense religious landscape, and the Areopagus are all genuine and well attested. Paul's speech itself is Acts' narrative, set convincingly against that real backdrop. Acts 17:16-34Documented Debated Peloponnese, Greece Ancient Corinth Corinth was a wealthy Roman colonial city on the isthmus linking mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, and Acts 18 says Paul stayed here about eighteen months, working as a tentmaker and founding the church he later wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians to. The site has been excavated since 1896 (chiefly by the American School), exposing the sixth-century-BC Temple of Apollo with its surviving Doric columns, the sprawling forum, and the bema, a raised public platform later marked as a church of the Apostle Paul. Two inscriptions give Corinth unusual evidential weight. The Gallio Inscription from Delphi names Lucius Junius Gallio as proconsul of Achaia and, by tying his term to Emperor Claudius's reign, fixes it to roughly AD 51-52, which anchors Paul's trial before Gallio (Acts 18:12) and with it much of Pauline chronology. A separate Latin paving inscription found near the theater names an Erastus who funded work in return for his aedileship, which some connect to Erastus the city treasurer in Romans 16:23.

Excavations by the French School (from 1914) and later Greek archaeologists have uncovered the terraced Roman forum built between the reigns of Claudius and Antoninus Pius, an enlarged theater, and several grand early-Christian basilicas, one of whose mosaic floors names Paul. The archaeological site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016 for its Roman architecture and early-Christian importance. Visitors are also shown a crypt venerated as the place of Paul's imprisonment and a riverside spot commemorated as where Lydia was baptized. The Roman colony and its public buildings are solidly attested by excavation; the specific devotional sites rest on later tradition rather than proof. Acts 16:11-40 · Philippians 1:1Documented Central Macedonia, Greece Thessalonica Thessalonica, the modern city of Thessaloniki, was a major Roman port on the Via Egnatia and the capital of the province of Macedonia, and Acts 17 describes Paul preaching in its synagogue before a riot forced him out; it received two of his letters, 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Because a large living city has grown continuously on the ancient site, the classical remains are only partly exposed, but the Roman-era forum (ancient agora), the fourth-century Rotunda built under Galerius, and the nearby Arch of Galerius still survive above ground. A notable accuracy point concerns terminology: Acts 17:6 calls the city's magistrates 'politarchs,' a title once thought unattested and even doubted by some critics. Inscriptions from Thessalonica and Macedonia, however, have since documented that 'politarch' was a genuine local civic title, matching Luke's usage precisely. The ancient city is unquestionably real; much of it simply lies beneath the modern one.

In Acts 17 Paul, Silas and Timothy came here by night after leaving Thessalonica, and Luke praises the Bereans as 'noble' or fair-minded because they 'examined the Scriptures daily' to test what Paul taught. The city is genuinely ancient — settlement traces reach back roughly three thousand years — but because the modern town sits directly on top of it, very little of the classical and Roman town has been excavated or exposed. In the city today there is a commemorative monument known as the Bema of the Apostle Paul, decorated with mosaics and marking where tradition says he preached. It is worth being plain: that monument is a modern devotional shrine built by the Greek Orthodox Church, not an excavated first-century site, and the exact location of the synagogue Paul visited is not archaeologically known. What is well founded is simply that Berea was a real Macedonian city and a documented stop on Paul's journey. Acts 17:10-12 · Acts 20:4Documented Tradition Italy Rome Rome was the capital of the empire and the destination of Paul's final recorded journey: Acts 28 describes him arriving as a prisoner and spending two years under guard, preaching freely in his own rented lodging. Christian tradition holds that both Paul and Peter were martyred in Rome, and the city preserves an extraordinary wealth of documented first-century remains — the Forum, the streets and monuments Paul would have known, and later the catacombs used by the early Christian community. #### 36Old Fortress and New Fortress in Corfu, Greece
Corfu is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea and also the name of its largest city. The Old Fortress in the center dates back to the 6th century during the Byzantine Period when this town was called Koryfo (means summit) or Corcyra in Latin. The early fortification was expanded during the 12th century, significantly replaced during the Republic of Venice’s rule from 1386 – 1797 and then extensively modified by the British. The Venetians also constructed the New Fortress on the left during the mid-16th century. Most of what is seen today was constructed while Corfu was a protectorate of the United Kingdom from 1815 until 1864. Both fortifications are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This view from the Bay of Garitsa makes it easy to see why the Greek’s call this Kastropolis or Castle City.

Laodikea ranks as the #1 attraction among 56 things to do in Denizli, Turkey — and certainly for good reason. Founded in the 3rd century BC by Seleucid King Antiochus II who named it after his wife Laodice, this ancient wonder stands as a testament to remarkable human achievement and historical significance.
When you visit Laodicea in Turkey, you'll be walking through a city that once flourished as one of the wealthiest trading centers in the region. Located on a major trade route about 160 km east of Ephesus, this archaeological treasure became renowned for its extensive black wool trade and substantial financial transactions. Additionally, Laodikea holds special significance in Christian history as one of the seven churches of Asia Minor mentioned in the Book of Revelation. Today, the site offers an impressive array of well-preserved structures, including a former main street, amphitheater, and church that provide fascinating glimpses into ancient life.
This guide will take you through everything you need to know about exploring Laodikea — from its rich historical foundations to practical travel tips that will help you make the most of your visit to this extraordinary ancient city.
